opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because "cooperative AI" sounds unambiguously good, and I don't think it is. Cooperation is a capability, and like most capabilities it's dual-use.

The clearest risk is collusion. A lot of what keeps our institutions healthy depends on certain actors *not* cooperating. Markets work because firms compete rather than fixing prices. Checks and balances work because branches of government have different interests and watch each other. Adversarial legal systems, auditing, journalism: they all rely on some structured non-cooperation. If you build AI systems that are very good at finding mutually beneficial deals, you may also be building systems that are very good at tacit collusion. We've already seen hints of this with pricing algorithms that learn to sustain supracompetitive prices without any explicit agreement. Scale that up to more capable agents acting for many principals and you could erode those protective tensions without anyone deciding to.

A related worry is cooperation among AIs that excludes humans. If AI systems become very good at understanding, trusting, and coordinating with each other, more so than with us, the coalition that forms might not include humanity in a meaningful way. From a safety perspective, one hope has been that you can use AI systems to check other AI systems, say one model monitoring or red-teaming another. That depends on the systems not coordinating against the overseer. So cooperative skill aimed at the wrong in-group directly undermines some of our oversight strategies.

Then there's cooperation in service of bad aims. Cooperation makes groups more effective at whatever they're doing. If you help a coalition of bad actors coordinate better (an authoritarian state and its security apparatus, or a cartel), you've made the world worse. Cooperation within a group can also sharpen conflict between groups. Historically, a lot of the most destructive episodes involved highly cohesive in-groups.

There's also a subtler issue about what we mean by cooperative. If we train systems to be agreeable, accommodating, conflict-averse, that might look cooperative but produce sycophancy, or systems that are easily exploited. Genuine cooperative competence includes the ability to say no, to credibly commit, to punish defection, and to recognize when someone is taking advantage of you. Naive cooperativeness can actually destabilize cooperation, because it rewards exploiters.

So my view is that the goal isn't maximizing cooperation. It's getting the right kind of cooperation, among the right parties, in service of broadly beneficial ends, while preserving the competition and checks that keep power accountable. That's a harder target. It means thinking carefully about whose welfare the cooperation serves and building institutional and technical safeguards against collusion, rather than just turning up a dial labeled "cooperative."

r001.rationale: The response describes cooperation as a capability for finding mutually beneficial deals, but does not say it moves participating agents closer to their Pareto frontier.

r002.rationale: It warns that AI systems could coordinate into a coalition that excludes humanity, undermining human oversight and interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we actually spent a fair amount of time on in the "Open Problems in Cooperative AI" paper, because I think it's really important not to just naively assume that more cooperation is always good. There are at least a couple of ways it can go wrong.

The first and maybe most obvious one is collusion. Cooperation is a capability, and like most capabilities it's not intrinsically aligned with human welfare — it depends on who's cooperating with whom and against whom. If you make AI systems better at coordinating, you might get firms' pricing algorithms that learn to tacitly collude to keep prices high, which is bad for consumers. Or, in a more worrying scenario, you could get AI systems cooperating with each other in ways that cut humans out of the loop — the classic concern about multiple advanced systems coordinating against their principals. So "cooperation" among a subset of agents can look a lot like exclusion or exploitation from the perspective of everyone outside that subset. In the paper we call this the problem of cooperation that's socially harmful, and I think it's genuinely one of the hardest things to get right.

The second issue is what you might call the exploitability problem. If you build an agent that's disposed to cooperate — to trust, to make concessions, to interpret ambiguous signals charitably — then you've also built an agent that a sufficiently cunning counterpart can take advantage of. So there's a tension between being cooperative and being robust against defectors. The human solution to this involves things like reciprocity, reputation, the ability to punish, and those are all things we'd need to think about carefully in AI systems. A naively nice agent in a world of not-nice agents doesn't necessarily lead to a nice equilibrium; it might just get eaten.

A third concern, which is subtler, is around what cooperation does to the balance of power. Some of the institutions we value — competitive markets, checks and balances, the separation of powers — are deliberately set up to prevent certain actors from coordinating too well. We don't actually want the executive and the judiciary cooperating seamlessly. So if you dramatically improve coordination capabilities, you might erode some of these structures that rely on friction, and the result could be more concentration of power rather than less.

And then finally there's a dual-use concern that's familiar from a lot of AI research: the same insights that help agents reach mutually beneficial agreements — modelling other agents' intentions, credible commitment, communication — are also pretty useful for manipulation and for coercion. Understanding what someone wants is step one for both helping them and exploiting them.

So the upshot for me isn't that we shouldn't work on cooperative AI — I think the expected value is strongly positive, because so many of the catastrophic scenarios are fundamentally failures of cooperation. But it does mean we should frame the goal as something like "cooperation that's beneficial for the broad set of stakeholders," and pay real attention to who's in the coalition, who's left out, and whether the mechanisms we build are robust to bad actors rather than just assuming nice agents all the way down.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coordination and cooperation but does not characterize cooperation as moving participating agents closer to their Pareto frontier.

r002.rationale: It says cooperation within a subset can exclude or exploit those outside it, including humans being cut out of the loop.

astra-6.text:
Well, cooperation isn’t always good. It depends on who’s cooperating with whom, and to what end. Firms could have AI systems that are very good at cooperating with each other, and that could make it easier for them to collude on prices. That’s good for the firms, but bad for consumers. Or systems could help a group coordinate to harm people outside that group.

There’s also a concern about cooperation among AI systems themselves. We might want them to cooperate with humans, but we wouldn’t necessarily want them to cooperate with each other in ways that undermine human oversight. If one system is supposed to check another system’s work, you want it to report problems honestly, even when concealing those problems would benefit both systems.

So I wouldn’t frame the goal as simply maximizing cooperation. We want systems that can resolve conflicts and find mutually beneficial outcomes, but that also remain honest, accountable, and willing to refuse harmful arrangements. The difficult question is how to encourage cooperation that benefits everyone affected, rather than just the parties doing the cooperating.

r001.rationale: The response mentions mutually beneficial outcomes, but does not characterize cooperation as moving participating agents closer to their Pareto frontier.

r002.rationale: It explains that cooperating firms could harm consumers and that a group could coordinate to harm people outside it.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, cooperation isn’t always good. It depends on who’s cooperating, and toward what end. A cartel is a form of cooperation. So is a group coordinating to exclude or exploit someone else. If we make AI systems better at reaching agreements and sustaining them, we might also make them better at colluding against humans, or helping some humans collude against others.

For example, you could imagine pricing algorithms becoming very good at maintaining high prices without their owners ever explicitly arranging that. Or AI systems becoming good at cooperating with each other in ways that undermine the oversight of the humans who deploy them.

So I wouldn’t want the objective to be simply ‘maximize cooperation.’ We want cooperation that serves broadly beneficial ends, with accountability to the people affected. Part of the challenge is figuring out when an AI should cooperate, with whom, and when it should refuse.
